problem: What is the horizontal asymptote of $y=f(x)$ for $x<0$ with $f(x)=\frac{|3x+6|}{x-4}?$

activity_context.topic_title: Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes of Rational Functions

examples.knowledge_point: Identifying the Horizontal Asymptote of a Rational Function
examples.problem: What is the horizontal asymptote of $y=f(x)$ with $f(x)=\dfrac{2x^3+1}{x^3-15x}?$
examples.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote is $y=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x^3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{3}-15x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{15x}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(2+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})}{(1-\frac{15}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{2+0}{1-0} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2.$

feedback.worked_solution:
First, we divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{2}.$ Then, by noting that the reciprocals shrink to $0$ in the limit, we can then evaluate the resulting expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,\frac{-{x}^{6}+4x}{{x}^{2}+5} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,\frac{(\frac{-{x}^{6}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{4x}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{5}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,\frac{(-{x}^{4}+\frac{4}{x})}{(1+\frac{5}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,\frac{(-{x}^{4}+0)}{(1+0)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,-{x}^{4} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$
